🚀 NATO gambles on private contractors as space arms race heats up
In a push to beef up its military satellite constellation, NATO is drafting private rockets and spaceports into the effort—and getting ready to dole out billions in new contracts. The alliance has just unveiled two programs designed to draw industry deeper into the fold, Bloomberg reports.
🔴 The first, Starlift, will act as a brokerage that aggregates military demand and matches it with commercial launch providers operating from spaceports in NATO countries and South Korea. It will also develop and test procedures for short-notice launches—a capability that a crisis could demand.
🔴 The second program, the Global Data Marketplace, is a joint effort with the US Space Force. Alliance members will use it to purchase commercial space data and services. More than 200 companies are already on board, and roughly 300 others have been flagged as possible participants
NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska presented both initiatives at the opening of the the bloc’s Edge technology conference in Izmir, Turkey. A NATO official said the alliance has handled spaceports much like civilian labs or commercial airports until now, and needs to start treating them as strategic infrastructure on par with military air bases, with protection and backup capacity to match.
The commercial shift reaches beyond launch. The NATO Communications and Information Agency intends to award about $3.1 billion in private contracts over the next two years, some of it to commercial space firms. The rest will go toward cloud, artificial intelligence, cyber, command-and-control and network systems.
The initiatives arrive as space becomes an increasingly contested [military domain](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77727). The US acknowledged in September that it operates weapons [in orbit](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76712), and Russia, China and India have all demonstrated anti-satellite capabilities. NATO itself declared space an operational domain in 2019 and has said attacks to, from or within space could trigger its Article 5 collective-defense clause.

🇮🇷🛢🇺🇸 Iran keeps US forces at bay in Hormuz, turning blockade into costly standoff
Iran is widening its strikes across the Gulf, targeting Bahrain, home to the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an American airbase in Kuwait.
The escalation follows nearly two months of relative calm, according to the Associated Press. The recent strikes followed US attacks on what media reports describe as an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island. The US has also targeted Iranian communications towers and continued drone surveillance across the region – at a growing cost, with the IRGC reporting an increasing number of [downed American UAVs](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77920).
👉 Strait of Hormuz
Tankers continue to catch fire in the Strait of Hormuz. On November 16, two oil tankers reportedly struck naval mines while attempting to cross a route Iran had not authorized.
Between March 1 and November 11, the UN’s International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East. Meanwhile, the Strait of Hormuz Live Tracker shows oil and petroleum product flows through the strategic waterway continuing to [shrink](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77856).
👉 US naval presence
Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) says the US naval presence across the Gulf of Oman, Arabian Sea, Red Sea and Mediterranean now exceeds the levels seen during Operation Epic Fury.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt has joined the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the region. Remarkably, however, the Israeli think tank’s interactive map shows no US warships currently deployed in the Persian Gulf or Strait of Hormuz – a picture that supports Iranian statements that American vessels are keeping their distance from Iranian missiles.
👉 Calibrated escalation?
Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of “deliberate, calibrated escalation” to “steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade,” INSS’s Danny Citrinowicz wrote on X. He outlined two possible paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a US decision to lift the blockade.
Meanwhile, geopolitical analyst Brandon Weichert warns on X that claims of an alleged Iranian dirty-bomb plot is likely an Israeli attempt to reignite the war.

🇵🇰 Pakistan test-fires Fatah-3 supersonic cruise missile
The missile is designed for long-range precision strikes and will extend the reach of Pakistan’s Army Rocket Force Command, the military’s media wing said after the successful Nov. 18 launch.
Defense outlet Quwa sees the Fatah-3 as Pakistan’s counterpart to India’s BrahMos and identifies land attack and potential anti-ship roles. It estimates a cruise speed of Mach 2.2–3.5, using China’s HD-1A as a benchmark. Pakistan’s launch announcement described the missile as supersonic and gave no exact speed or range.
The launch follows an October [test of the Fatah-2 hypersonic ballistic missile](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77266) and a flight test earlier this month of the Fa’az, Pakistan’s first domestically developed air-to-air missile.
